title: Do all ACL tears need surgery?
d: No. Many active people choose ACL reconstruction, especially for sports with pivoting and cutting. Some people do well with rehab alone, particularly if they don't play pivoting sports. Your surgeon and physical therapist can help you decide.

title: How long is recovery after ACL reconstruction?
d: Most people walk normally within a few weeks and return to running after a few months. Return to pivoting sports usually takes at least about nine months, once strength and movement tests show the knee is ready.

title: Does an MCL tear need surgery?
d: Usually not. Most MCL sprains heal with a period of protection, often a brace, and a progressive rehab program.

title: Can physical therapy help before ACL surgery?
d: Yes. Getting swelling down, restoring full motion and building strength before reconstruction is linked with a smoother recovery afterward.

title: Should I rest a sprained ankle completely?
d: Usually not for long. After the first few days, gentle movement and walking as pain allows help a sprain heal. A physical therapist can guide you on when to add balance and strengthening work.

title: Why does my ankle keep rolling?
d: After a sprain, the ankle's strength and balance reactions often don't fully recover on their own, which makes another sprain more likely. Balance and strength training can reduce that risk.

title: Should I stop running with Achilles pain?
d: Not always. Many people can keep some running or walking while the tendon gets stronger, as long as pain stays mild and settles by the next day. Your therapist will help you adjust your training.

title: How long does Achilles tendon pain take to get better?
d: Tendons improve slowly. Many people notice progress within several weeks of consistent loading exercise, with full recovery taking a few months. Sticking with the program is what makes the difference.

d: Gentle breathing, walking and posture work can often start in the early weeks as you feel ready. Many women begin physical therapy after their postpartum check, once their provider has checked the incision.

title: Is numbness around my C-section scar normal?

d: Groin pain when you walk, stiffness putting on socks, or an aching outer hip that's worse lying on that side at night. Strengthening the hip and thigh muscles is a strongly recommended treatment for hip arthritis and painful outer-hip tendons.

title: Knee arthritis and knee pain
d: Pain on stairs, stiffness after sitting, or a knee that swells after a busy day. Exercise-based physical therapy is one of the most strongly recommended treatments for knee osteoarthritis, and for some people it can put off the need for surgery.

title: ACL and MCL knee ligament injuries
d: A twist or pop, then swelling or a knee that gives way. Most MCL sprains heal without surgery, and rehab is central to ACL recovery, with or without reconstruction, and to a safe return to sport.

title: Plantar fasciitis and heel pain
d: Sharp pain in the bottom of your heel with your first steps in the morning or after sitting. Hands-on therapy, stretching, taping, strengthening and footwear advice treat it without injections or surgery for most people.

title: Ankle sprains and Achilles pain
d: A rolled ankle that stays weak or keeps giving way, or Achilles pain that's worst with your first steps in the morning. Balance training after a sprain lowers the chance of another one, and progressive strengthening is the first treatment for Achilles pain.

title: Pulled muscles and muscle strains
d: A sudden grab in the hamstring, calf, groin or back mid-activity. Early gentle movement and progressive strengthening heal strains and help stop the same muscle going again.

title: Bladder leaks (urinary incontinence)
d: Leaking when you cough, sneeze, laugh, lift or exercise, or sudden urges you can't hold. Supervised pelvic floor muscle training is recommended as a first treatment for stress and mixed incontinence in women, before medication or surgery.

title: Accidental bowel leakage
d: Leaking gas or stool, or urgency you can't hold, often after childbirth or around menopause. Pelvic floor training and bowel habit changes are a recommended first treatment.

title: Pelvic organ prolapse
d: A feeling of heaviness, pressure or bulging in the vagina, often after childbirth or menopause and worse at the end of the day. Supervised pelvic floor muscle training is recommended for symptoms of mild to moderate prolapse, along with lifting and bowel habits that reduce strain.

title: Pelvic pain and painful sex
d: Pain with intercourse, pelvic or tailbone pain, or pain with tampons or exams is often linked to pelvic floor muscles that are tight or overworked. Pelvic floor therapy helps these muscles relax and work properly, gently and at your pace, in a private room.

title: Interstitial cystitis and bladder pain
d: Bladder pain, pressure and frequent urges when tests keep coming back clear. Gentle pelvic floor therapy to relax tight muscles is recommended, rather than Kegels.

title: Diastasis recti (separated abdominal muscles)
d: A gap or bulge down the middle of your belly after pregnancy, sometimes with low back pain or a “pooch” that exercise hasn't fixed. Physical therapy retrains your deep core and pelvic floor to work together so you can return to exercise with confidence.

title: Back and pelvic pain during pregnancy
d: Pain in the low back, at the back of the pelvis or at the pubic bone, often worse turning in bed, on stairs or standing on one leg. Gentle, one-on-one prenatal physical therapy eases pain and keeps you moving, adjusted to each trimester.

title: C-section recovery
d: Scar tightness or numbness, a weak core, back pain, or trouble lifting your baby after a cesarean. Physical therapy helps you heal, rebuild your core and pelvic floor, and return to exercise.

title: Vertigo and dizziness (BPPV)
d: The room spins for a few seconds when you roll over in bed, lie down or look up. This is often BPPV, the most common cause of vertigo, and repositioning treatment by a trained physical therapist often helps within a few visits.

title: Balance problems and fall prevention
d: Feeling unsteady, holding onto furniture, or afraid of falling again. Balance can be trained at any age, and exercise programs that build balance and leg strength reduce falls in older adults.

title: TMJ and jaw pain
d: Aching in the jaw or temples, painful clicking, trouble opening wide, or clenching and grinding. Gentle hands-on care, jaw and neck exercises and habit changes are an effective first treatment for most TMJ problems.

title: Osteoporosis and bone health
d: If you've been told you have osteopenia or osteoporosis, the right exercise matters. Physical therapy teaches safe strengthening and weight-bearing exercise, balance training to lower your risk of falls, and ways to move that protect your spine.

title: Recovery after a broken bone
d: Stiff and weak after a cast, boot or fracture surgery. Rehab restores motion, strength and walking while following your doctor's instructions for the healing bone.

title: Getting stronger before surgery (prehab)
d: Building strength and motion before a planned knee, hip or shoulder surgery, learning the exercises you'll use afterward, and preparing your home and routine, so recovery starts on a better footing.

title: Knee and hip replacement rehab
d: Getting your new knee to bend and straighten, walking without a walker or limp, and handling stairs and the car again. One-on-one rehab that follows your surgeon's plan and precautions.

title: Rotator cuff repair and shoulder surgery rehab
d: Protecting the repair while it heals, then bringing back motion and strength, step by step with your surgeon's protocol.

title: Back and neck surgery rehab
d: After a discectomy, laminectomy or fusion: a walking plan, trunk and leg strength, and safe ways to bend and lift within your surgeon's precautions.

title: Recovery after surgery
d: Rehabilitation after joint replacement, ACL and rotator cuff repair, spine surgery and more, coordinated with your surgeon's protocol.
